evidence: backend/crates/api-core/src/middleware/rls_context.rs:185-251 — `require_rls_context` is documented (lines 181-184) as 'a stricter version ... Use this for routes that MUST have tenant isolation', but it enforces NOTHING: it calls `db::tenant_context::set_request_context(pool.as_ref(), Some(tenant_id), Some(user_id), is_super_admin)` (line 232) then runs the handler via `next.run(request)` (line 245). `set_request_context<E: Executor>` (backend/crates/db/src/tenant_context.rs:18) issues its `set_config`/SET on a connection sqlx transiently checks out of the POOL and immediately returns; the handler later acquires a DIFFERENT pooled connection where the RLS GUCs are unset. Result: tenant-isolation is silently NOT applied to the handler's queries — a cross-tenant data-exposure footgun for any route that adopts this middleware believing the doc.

The module's own header (rls_context.rs:1-37) already diagnoses this exact defect ('Setting RLS on the pool doesn't affect individual connections'; 'PostgreSQL session settings are connection-scoped, not pool-scoped') and marks the module DEPRECATED — yet the file is not `#[deprecated]`, and BOTH broken functions plus `rls_context_middleware` are glob re-exported to consumers via `pub use rls_context::*;` (backend/crates/api-core/src/middleware/mod.rs:16). The contradiction (top says 'do NOT use'; `require_rls_context` docstring says 'use this for routes that MUST have tenant isolation') is the trap.

Not currently mounted in either server (grep of servers/ finds no call site), so severity is a LATENT bypass rather than a live one — hence confidence medium, not high. But it is live-ready API surface: a future route author who follows the `require_rls_context` docstring gets a compiling, plausible-looking guard that leaks across tenants with no error.

Fix: delete the deprecated module (the correct path is the `RlsConnection` extractor, which sets RLS on the same dedicated connection it hands the handler — see extractors/rls_connection.rs), or at minimum stop re-exporting it and add `#[deprecated]` + `compile_error!`-style guards; do NOT leave a function named `require_rls_context` that provides no isolation.

backend/crates/api-core/src/middleware/authorization.rs:170-201 — `require_permission` derives the caller role with `request.extensions().get::<TenantRole>().cloned().unwrap_or(TenantRole::Guest)` (lines 176-180). For an UNAUTHENTICATED request (no `TenantRole` in extensions) the role defaults to `Guest`, whose `level()` is 10 (backend/crates/common/src/tenant.rs:125).

`require_authenticated` (authorization.rs:236-241) delegates to `permissions::AUTHENTICATED = Permission::min_level(1, ...)` (line 139). `is_satisfied_by(Guest)` = `Guest.level() >= 1` = `10 >= 1` = TRUE. So the middleware literally named 'require authenticated user' GRANTS access to a request that carries NO authenticated identity — a fail-OPEN default. The higher-tier convenience guards (require_manager=80, require_owner=60, require_admin=90) happen to still deny Guest, so the hole is specific to the AUTHENTICATED gate, i.e. exactly the guard a route would pick to mean 'any logged-in user'.

Currently these from_fn-style guards are not mounted in servers/ (routes use their own `require_manager_in_org`/`require_platform_admin` helpers), so this is a latent footgun, not a live bypass — confidence medium. But it is public, documented, example-carrying middleware inviting adoption.

Fix: make the missing-role case fail closed — return 401 when no `TenantRole` (or authenticated principal) is present instead of substituting `Guest`, and/or give unauthenticated requests a role whose level is 0 that no `min_level(1)` permission satisfies. An authorization primitive must never treat 'no identity' as a valid low-privilege identity that clears an 'authenticated' check.

backend/crates/api-core/src/middleware/idempotency.rs:95-179 — `handle_idempotent_request` opens a DB transaction `pool.begin()` (line 95), takes a `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (line 108), and then HOLDS that transaction (and therefore one pooled connection) open across the entire downstream request: `next.run(request).await` at line 148, committing only afterward (line 177). The wrapped handler independently acquires its OWN pooled connection(s) (e.g. via the `RlsConnection` extractor) to do its work.

Concurrency hazard: with pool size N, N concurrent idempotent requests (distinct keys) each pin one connection in the still-open idempotency transaction and then each block waiting to check out a second connection for their handler — a classic pool-exhaustion self-deadlock; all N stall until acquire timeouts fire. Even below saturation this doubles the effective connection footprint of every idempotent (mutating POST/PUT) request and stretches the advisory-lock/transaction hold time to the full handler latency (including any slow outbound calls the handler makes).

The extensive comment at lines 80-94 justifies the xact-scoped lock purely for cancellation-safety (leak avoidance) and does NOT acknowledge the connection-held-across-handler cost, suggesting the pool-pressure interaction was not considered.

Fix: don't straddle the handler with an open transaction. Acquire the advisory lock + look up/insert a 'pending' ledger row in a SHORT transaction that commits before `next.run`, then persist the captured response in a SECOND short transaction after the handler returns (serialization is still provided by the ledger row / a shorter-lived lock). This releases the connection for the duration of handler execution and removes the deadlock/footprint-doubling.
